title: Find First and Last Position of Element in Sorted Array
description:
# Find First and Last Position of Element in Sorted Array

Given an integer array `nums` sorted in non-decreasing order and an integer `target`, return the first and last index where `target` appears.

If `target` does not appear in `nums`, return `[-1, -1]`.

Use `O(log n)` time, where `n` is the array length.

## Example 1

**Input:** nums = [5,7,7,8,8,10], target = 8

**Output:** [3,4]

## Example 2

**Input:** nums = [5,7,7,8,8,10], target = 6

**Output:** [-1,-1]

## Example 3

**Input:** nums = [], target = 0

**Output:** [-1,-1]

## Constraints

* `0 <= nums.length <= 100000`
* `-1000000000 <= nums[i] <= 1000000000`
* `nums` is sorted in non-decreasing order.
* `-1000000000 <= target <= 1000000000`

solutions.name: Two Boundary Binary Searches
solutions.description:
## Approach

Run one closed-interval binary search that keeps the best left boundary seen so far, then run a second closed-interval binary search that keeps the best right boundary seen so far.

## Key Insight

Finding one occurrence is not the same as finding the range. When `nums[mid] == target`, the left-boundary search must continue left, while the right-boundary search must continue right.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(log n)
- Space Complexity: O(1)

solutions.name: Lower Bound and Upper Bound
solutions.description:
## Approach

Compute `lowerBound(target)`, the first index whose value is greater than or equal to `target`, and `upperBound(target)`, the first index whose value is greater than `target`. The target range is `[lower, upper - 1]` if `lower` points to the target.

## Key Insight

A duplicate range can be described as the gap between two insertion positions. Using an upper-bound helper avoids overflow-sensitive tricks such as searching for `target + 1`.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(log n)
- Space Complexity: O(1)

solutions.name: Find One Occurrence Then Binary Boundaries
solutions.description:
## Approach

First run ordinary binary search to locate any occurrence of `target`. If one exists, binary search only the left side for the first occurrence and only the right side for the last occurrence.

## Key Insight

The common mistake is to expand linearly from the found index. Keeping both boundary refinements as binary searches preserves the required `O(log n)` time even when the whole array equals `target`.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(log n)
- Space Complexity: O(1)

solutions.name: Recursive Lower and Upper Bounds
solutions.description:
## Approach

Use recursion to compute the lower bound and upper bound over half-open intervals. After the recursive lower bound returns, verify the target exists, then derive the last index from the recursive upper bound.

## Key Insight

Both boundaries are first-position problems: first value greater than or equal to `target`, and first value greater than `target`. The same divide-and-conquer shape handles both.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(log n)
- Space Complexity: O(log n)
